The Story of Brahma's Austerity

I bow to Lord Adinath, the first Tirthankara, worshipped by the world, and I write the story of the divine being Brahma.

Some people say that one day Brahma conceived the desire to seize the position of Indra and become supreme. To this end, he performed terrible austerity in a fearsome forest, standing on one leg for four and a half thousand divine years, sustained only by air. His penance was not in vain — the thrones of Indra and the other gods began to tremble. They feared losing their kingdoms and sent a celestial courtesan named Tilottama, who danced and sang like the Gandharvas, to break his meditation.

Tilottama came and began to dance before Brahma with every manner of alluring gesture. Seeing her beauty and her enchanting movements, Brahma's millennia of austerity crumbled in a single moment. He surrendered himself to desire and began staring at Tilottama with wide, greedy eyes. When she saw that the yogi was no longer master of himself, she moved to his left side to further awaken his desire. Brahma, by the residual power of his penance, created a second face on his left side. When Tilottama danced behind him, he created a third face. When she moved to his right, he created a fourth. Finally, Tilottama rose into the sky and danced above him — and Brahma created a fifth face, shaped like a donkey's muzzle, for by now the fruit of his austerity was nearly exhausted.

The point is that Tilottama made Brahma dance just as she pleased. Having broken his penance and set his heart ablaze with desire, the clever Tilottama flew back to heaven untouched, while poor Brahma swooned in the fierce grip of lust.

This story is told to reveal the absurdity of worshipping such beings as supreme creators. A being who claims to be the lord of all creation is undone by a single dancer. He grows donkey faces trying to ogle her. His thousands of years of austerity are destroyed in a moment of weakness. Can such a being be the creator and ruler of the universe? Can one who is a slave to desire be worthy of worship?

The Jain tradition asks these questions not to mock but to encourage discernment. True divinity is found not in beings who create and destroy through whimsy, but in those who have conquered all passions — who are free from anger, pride, deceit, and greed. The Jinas, who have destroyed all karmas and attained infinite knowledge, vision, bliss, and power — they alone are worthy of worship, for they show the path that leads beyond all suffering.
